A1.title: Nouns · Gender and singular/plural
A1.rule: Learn each noun with its gender and plural form. Many masculine nouns end in a consonant, many feminine nouns in -a and many neuter nouns in -o or -e. These are clues. For example, mężczyzna is masculine despite ending in -a.

tables.title: Gender and number in the nominative

A1.title: Adjectives · Gender and number
A1.rule: The adjective follows the gender and number of its noun. Compare mały, mała and małe in the singular. In the nominative plural, małe is used with things and mali with masculine-personal nouns such as chłopcy.

tables.title: Nominative agreement
rows: małe domy / małe torby / małe okna

A1.title: Nominative and adjective agreement
A1.rule: Use the nominative for the subject and to identify something after to jest. Match the adjective to the noun's gender and number.

tables.title: Nominative agreement
rows: małe domy / małe torby / małe okna

A1.title: Verbs · Six persons in the present
A1.rule: First learn the forms of czytać for all six persons. The ending often tells you who is doing the action. In everyday Polish, subject pronouns such as ja and my can be left out when the context makes them clear.

examples.english: You are reading a newspaper. (one person)
The child is reading a story. The neuter noun dziecko takes the same form as ono.
You read in Polish. (more than one person)
They read in the library. (e.g. a group of women)

A1.title: Verbs · Być and mieć
A1.rule: Learn these frequent verbs as complete patterns. In person order ja, ty, on/ona/ono, my, wy, oni/one: być has jestem, jesteś, jest, jesteśmy, jesteście, są. Mieć has mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają.

examples.english: Do you have tickets? (more than one person)

A1.title: Present tense
A1.rule: Czytać is imperfective. Use its present tense for what is happening now or what happens regularly. Polish has six person-and-number slots. On, ona and ono share one form, and oni and one share another. The subject pronoun is often omitted when the verb ending and context identify the subject.

examples.english: You are reading a newspaper. (one person)
The child is reading a story. The neuter noun dziecko takes the same form as ono.
You read in Polish. (more than one person)
They read in the library. (e.g. a group of women)

A1.title: Accusative and genitive
A1.rule: A direct object often takes the accusative. When you negate a verb whose direct object takes the accusative, that object generally takes the genitive.

A1.title: Noun and adjective · Object and negation
A1.rule: Practise the whole phrase. With mieć, a direct object takes the accusative. After nie mieć, it takes the genitive. Change both the adjective and the noun where required.

examples.english: I don't have a new book.
I don't have a small dog. (Here the accusative and genitive look the same.)
I don't have a new bicycle.

A1.title: Instrumental and locative
A1.rule: Use the instrumental for a profession after być. Use the locative after w or na to say where something is in these examples.

examples.english: The keys are on the table.

tables.title: From the base phrase to the case form

A1.title: Noun and adjective · With someone or in a place
A1.rule: Use the instrumental after z when it means with. Use the locative after w and na in these examples of location. The adjective changes with the noun.

examples.english: I'm going with a good friend.
I'm talking to the new neighbour.
We live in a small town.
The phone is lying on the big table.

tables.title: From the base phrase to the case form

A1.title: Nouns · Giving and addressing
A1.rule: Use the dative for the person receiving something. Use the vocative to address someone directly. Start with familiar forms, then compare all seven cases in Reference · Noun declension.

A1.title: Verbs · First look at past and future
A1.rule: Compare three everyday time words. In the past, czytałem and czytałam differ by the speaker's gender. For the future of czytać, you can start with będę plus the infinitive.

examples.english: I read a book yesterday. (male speaker)
I read a book yesterday. (female speaker)

A2.title: Dative and vocative
A2.rule: Use the dative for a recipient or after verbs such as pomagać. Use the vocative when directly addressing someone.

examples.english: I'm giving my brother a ticket.

A2.title: Location and destination
A2.rule: With na, the locative can describe where you are and the accusative can describe where you are going.

examples.english: I'm going to the post office.

A2.title: Past and future
A2.rule: In the singular past, the form can depend on the subject's gender. For the imperfective future, use a form of być plus the infinitive or the matching past-type form.

examples.english: I read a book yesterday. (female speaker)
I read a book yesterday. (male speaker)
I'll read a book tomorrow. (female speaker)

A2.title: Comparatives and superlatives
A2.rule: Use the comparative with niż to compare things. The superlative commonly adds naj- to the comparative.

examples.english: This ticket is cheaper than that one.
This hotel is better than the previous one.

B1.title: Verb aspect
B1.rule: The imperfective often presents an action as ongoing or repeated. The perfective presents it as a bounded event, often with a completed result.

examples.english: When you called, I was writing a report.
I'll have the report written by tomorrow.

B1.title: Cases required by verbs
B1.rule: Learn the case with the whole expression. Ufać takes the dative, unikać the genitive and interesować się the instrumental.

tables.title: Learn the case with the verb

B1.title: Relative clauses
B1.rule: Który agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to. Its case depends on its role within the relative clause.

examples.polish: To jest osoba, **która** pracuje w banku.
examples.english: This is the person who works at the bank.
This is the person I trust.
This is the person I work with.

tables.title: Relative pronoun · masculine person and feminine

B1.title: Conditional sentences
B1.rule: Use gdyby to introduce a hypothetical condition. In the result clause, a form such as pomógłbym combines the masculine past-type form with -bym.

examples.english: If I had time, I would help you. (male speaker)
If I had time, I would help you. (female speaker)

B2.title: Passive voice
B2.rule: Use być with an imperfective passive participle for an ongoing process in these examples. Zostać with a perfective passive participle presents the event as completed. The participle agrees with the subject.

examples.english: The report is being analysed by the committee.
The report was analysed by the committee.
The results will be published tomorrow.

B2.title: Adverbial participles
B2.rule: An imperfective -ąc participle indicates a simultaneous action. A perfective anterior participle in -wszy or -łszy indicates an earlier completed action. Both actions share the same subject.

examples.english: While reading the report, she noticed an error.
Having read the report, she sent her comments.

B2.title: Formal prepositions and cases
B2.rule: Learn formal expressions with the cases they govern. Wbrew takes the dative, wskutek the genitive and w związku z the instrumental.

examples.english: Contrary to earlier agreements, the date was changed.
The meeting was cancelled due to a breakdown.
The vote was postponed because of the delay.

B2.title: Linking ideas
B2.rule: Use mimo że to introduce a concession. Use im ..., tym ... to show that two things change together. Use czy for an indirect yes-or-no question.

examples.polish: **Mimo że** raport był gotowy, przełożono spotkanie.
examples.english: Although the report was ready, the meeting was postponed.

examples.polish: **Im** dłużej czekamy, **tym** trudniej będzie podjąć decyzję.
examples.english: The longer we wait, the harder it will be to make a decision.
It is unclear whether the committee will approve the project.

tables.title: Choose the connector by its job

reference.title: Reference · Noun declension
reference.rule: Each noun has a grammatical gender. Compare a masculine person (student), a masculine inanimate noun (stół), a feminine noun (książka) and a neuter noun (okno). These are model nouns. Endings and stem changes vary across nouns.

examples.english: I see a student and a table. The two masculine nouns differ in the singular accusative.
I am looking closely at the books. Książkom is dative plural.

reference.title: Reference · Adjective declension
reference.rule: A Polish adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In the singular accusative, masculine animate and inanimate forms differ. In the plural, compare masculine-personal and other nouns. For an adjective modifying a noun in direct address, the adjective’s vocative matches its nominative.

examples.english: I see a good student and a good table. Compare the two masculine accusatives.
I’m talking with good students. Both words are instrumental plural.

reference.title: Reference · Verb conjugation
reference.rule: Compare the imperfective czytać with the perfective przeczytać. The present exists for czytać. The corresponding simple forms of przeczytać refer to the future. Past and conditional forms distinguish gender. In the plural, compare masculine-personal forms (oni) with other forms (one). Imperatives are listed for the persons most commonly taught first.

examples.english: I read a book yesterday. (female speaker)
I’ll be reading a book tomorrow. (female speaker)
I’ll have read the book by Friday.
